opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Jasmine, thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, and we don't work for any company, union or party. Nothing you tell me will be linked to your name, so feel free to tell me what you'd say out loud and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, love this. Ask me anything. I've got opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say cool, but nobody wants to be served by a tablet. People come to a bar for the bartender.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it doesn't touch me. My worry is rent and slow Tuesdays, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working five nights, keep my regulars happy, try to save something for once. I use AI to help with my resume and cocktail ideas, that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty chill.

S0.say: Nobody wants to be served by a tablet. People come to a bar for the bartender.
S0.think: It doesn't touch her; rent and slow nights worry her more.
S0.do: Works five nights, keeps her regulars, tries to save, and uses AI for her resume and cocktail ideas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's messed up that companies stop hiring young people. That's how you get a whole generation stuck in service jobs, like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For my job, nothing. People still want a drink and a chat. But I've got the two-year degree and was thinking of going back for more. If entry jobs dry up, why bother?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay behind the bar, it's honestly safer than a desk now. Maybe do a proper bartending course to move to cocktail bars with better tips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. A bit annoyed for my friends.

S1.say: It's messed up that companies stop hiring young people. That's how a generation gets stuck in service jobs.
S1.think: Her job's untouched, but fewer entry jobs make going back to study look pointless.
S1.do: Stays behind the bar and takes a bartending course to move to higher-tip cocktail bars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say tax the companies doing the layoffs and give workers a real say. I'd post about it, go to the rallies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Office people are my best tippers at happy hour. If they're scared about their jobs, they order one drink, not three, and tip less. My income is tips. So yeah, it hits me sideways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pick up more weekend shifts when the money is better. Get involved with the hospitality workers' group in the city. Keep living with roommates, no way I'm moving out alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Mostly mad on other people's behalf.

S2.say: Tax the companies doing the layoffs and give workers a real say.
S2.think: Scared office workers drink less and tip less, which hits her income sideways.
S2.do: Takes more weekend shifts, joins a hospitality workers' group, and stays with roommates.
S2.feel: A bit uneasy, mostly angry for others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment. Billionaires get richer, everybody else gets fired. We need a wealth tax and basic income, now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job is weirdly safe. Rich people with booming shares drink a lot and tip well, and I'd move to a fancy bar to catch that. I'd feel gross about it, but I've got rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd serve the people you're protesting against. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. But that's always been the job. I've poured drinks for people I can't stand forever. At least I'd be taking their money for the cause.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get hired somewhere upscale, serve the people getting rich, and spend my days off organising. Probably canvass for whoever runs on taxing the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and kind of guilty, but energised.

S3.say: This is the moment. Billionaires get richer while everyone else gets fired. We need a wealth tax and basic income.
S3.think: Her job is oddly safe, and she'd chase tips from the newly rich, though she'd feel bad about it.
S3.do: Moves to an upscale bar, organises on days off, and canvasses for candidates who want to tax the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots in kitchens and care homes is where it gets inhuman. People need people. And the gains need to go to everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bars might be one of the last places with humans, honestly. But the kitchen staff I work with, the dishwashers, the cooks, they're gone. Restaurants with fewer staff close more often. My world gets a lot smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but I'd also start saving like crazy and look at a backup, maybe something in social work or organising as a real job. Push harder on the politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for me exactly, for everyone around me.

S4.say: Robots in kitchens and care homes is where it gets inhuman. People need people, and the gains must go to everyone.
S4.think: Bars may keep humans longest, but her kitchen coworkers would go and her world would shrink.
S4.do: Saves hard, looks at social work or organising as a paid backup, and pushes harder on the politics.
